The peculiar supernova SN~2020jfo has been studied in depth.  A detailed analysis of its elemental composition reveals an abundance of nickel that is 7.4 times greater than iron, a ratio significantly higher than the standard solar value of 6.3.  This ratio is exceptionally large, one of the highest ever observed in a supernova.  A thorough examination of previously studied supernovae, including those with similar spectral types, has shown that only one, SN~2004dj, has a nickel to iron ratio as high as SN~2020jfo's, and that ratio in SN~2020jfo is 1.5 times greater.  The unique characteristics of SN~2020jfo are further highlighted by a prolonged and strong [Fe~II] line, indicating that iron II is more abundant than iron I, a distinction seen in fewer than 5\% of the supernovae studied.  The rapid decline of SN~2020jfo also distinguishes it from other supernovae, with its magnitude dropping by 2.3 units in a span of fifty days, a rate significantly faster than the majority of Type~II supernovae. We introduced a new parameter, azimuthal rotation angle, to analyze lobster-eye optics images based on their symmetry, which is particularly effective for images with well-defined symmetry patterns, such as the cross-like image. By applying this parameter, we found that the MTF of a lobster-eye optics image varies significantly with the azimuthal rotation angle, providing valuable insights into how the MTF is affected by different parts of the optics system. For a lobster-eye optics with a radial groove pattern, we found that the MTF of the corresponding image is higher near the radial direction, which means that the azimuthal rotation angle can be used to identify different segments of the optics system. By simulating the point spread function of a lobster-eye optics system, which is based on a 12×12 μm pixel CMOS image sensor, we found that the MTF of the corresponding image is higher near the radial direction, which may help in self-correcting the MTF of the optics system.

This study presents a novel approach to solving a particular type of fully nonlinear equation of second order. Authors reformulate the problem as a level set evolution equation, which leads to multiple possible solutions. A key aspect of this method is the introduction of a new function, $H$, defined to detect changes in the sign of solutions. Combining $H$ with the distance function, authors derive a convergence result in the context of initial conditions with compact support. A further contribution of this research involves establishing the existence of solutions to the fully nonlinear equation of second order within convex domains.

To improve the accuracy of halo mass predictions, researchers are exploring alternative methods that bypass traditional density-only neural network models. However, our findings from cosmological simulations show that for a given set of parameters, models pre-trained on a density field can, in fact, enhance the accuracy of halo finding, specifically when the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations is high. To further investigate this observed effect, we modified the architecture of a proven halo finder by replacing its base model with the one trained on a density field, and assessed its performance on multiple simulation scenarios. Our experiments revealed that relative to a model trained on halo fields directly, there is an average 3.5% reduction in mass loss at the low-mass end (12 log M /M) and a 1.5% increase in mass gain at the high-mass end (13 log M /M), without any adjustment to the model's hyperparameters. Notably, when the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations is high, the difference in mass gain/loss can be as large as 5%/10% respectively. Our optimized model also demonstrates a higher level of robustness when exposed to simulations with different resolution and mass resolutions.

We present a novel approach to analyzing rotating stars through a mathematical technique called the method of averaging, which involves using the Eulerian perspective. This method assigns unique properties, such as mass and specific angular momentum, to individual fluid elements within the star, distinct from their individual trajectories. Contrary to conventional Eulerian methods, this approach can be used to solve both steady and dynamic problems involving rotating stars. Our study builds upon a previous work by Ogilvie and Taylor and involves deriving a new nonlinear averaged Euler equation. This equation includes a diffusion term that becomes significant at a critical point, leading to a non-monotonic behavior. It also leads to a 1.5-dimensional model equation when considering a specific narrow saturation criterion is met.

A popular and effective technique for reducing costs and time involved in creating labeled data is selective labeling. This approach involves allocating resources more efficiently by labeling only the most costly or difficult data, which has a greater impact on the model's performance when labeled. Although beneficial, integrating selective labeling into the supervised learning framework presents a challenge, as it requires assigning a label to a specific subset of training data. To address this issue, we developed a method called cost-sensitive pseudo-labeling, which assigns a label to an unlabelled sample based on the model's confidence and the data collection costs. This approach was tested and evaluated using two datasets, Adult and CreditCard, and the results showed that it can effectively reduce data costs by prioritizing the labeling of difficult data. Furthermore, our method was found to be a suitable alternative for comparing and evaluating the performance of automatic data labeling techniques.

The observation of LIGO/VIRGO gravitational waves from the merger of neutron stars, known as GW170817, has revolutionized the field of high-energy physics and astronomy.  Despite this discovery, the limited data set has hindered a comprehensive analysis of the phenomena associated with neutron star mergers.  A detailed study of GW170817 is conducted, incorporating newly available information from high-energy radiation observations.  By analyzing the behavior of a low-density neutron star crust in the post-merger phase, combined with constraints from electromagnetic observations, the study infers the presence of a strong shock wave that likely generated fast neutron rich matter that may have influenced the formation of heavy elements.  Additionally, the research implies that a high-density neutron star or black hole may have formed as a result of the merger, which could be confirmed through future electromagnetic and gravitational wave observations.

This research examines the lasting impact of the pandemic on diversity in urban meetings and community resilience in Toronto. We analyzed an extensive dataset containing information about diversity in encounters and community resilience gathered from over 1000 Torontonians between 2021 and 2022. Key findings show that diversity in urban meetings dropped significantly during lockdowns and recovered only partially after their lifting. Furthermore, our data reveal that community resilience, understood as the ability to adapt to challenges and support local communities, increased substantially throughout this period. However, our results also indicate that an overreaction to declining diversity in meetings might lead to misguided policies that underprioritize community resilience. We contend that a more effective approach for promoting diversity in urban meetings is one that also fosters community resilience.

Observations from recent studies have revealed that migrating objects in circumstellar disks around young, massive stars may become stuck or switch direction in the inner regions. A theoretical model proposes that this behavior is influenced by a balance of gravitational forces from dense disk particles and a gravitational interaction that occurs when fast-moving particles from the outer disk migrate inward. Using this framework, researchers simulated migrating objects in two specific types of inner disks: one composed of small particles that can stick together and another made up of larger particles that don't combine. By comparing these scenarios to observations, the study found that only the model featuring objects that don't merge correctly matches the observed patterns of migrating objects in the MKT-10 star's inner disk. Furthermore, the data and model indicate that the inner disk of this star spans approximately 1-3 solar radii in size and where the stars' strong gravitational pull starts to take effect. Notably, this is the first time that the size of a inner disk has been determined through direct observations of migrating objects.

This research paper formulates a new approach to solve a problem in water wave theory. By assuming that the surface elevation can be expressed in terms of a Jacobi elliptic function, an alternative method is proposed for reconstructing the surface elevation from the wave envelope, allowing for the derivation of an explicit formula for the velocity potential. Consequently, this method enables the direct computation of velocity and height statistics for water waves.

This expository article explains how the surface layer theorem facilitates the comprehension of differential forms within locally convex spaces. To begin, we outline the fundamental concepts and then delve into the specifics of the surface layer theorem. Next, we discuss the Dewynk's significant contribution that generalizes the surface layer theorem, showing how it enables the analysis of differential forms. Furthermore, we discuss recent findings and advancements made by Dewynk and others.

A novel layered control framework is presented for a mobile robot equipped with sonar sensors. The robot's movement is controlled at two levels: a higher-level path-planning module makes navigation decisions based on sensor data, while a lower-level module is responsible for speed and steering. The dynamic model is represented using a system of nonlinear differential equations, with the goal of maintaining a safe distance from obstacles. The performance of the controller is evaluated in a simulated environment, and subsequently refined through genetic algorithm optimization. The controller's effectiveness is demonstrated in a realistic scenario with multiple moving targets.

Reducing the impact of media bias in Automatic Fake News Detection using Multi-task Learning was investigated in our research. We developed a method where multiple tasks are balanced to minimize the effect of bias in the data. This approach considers three tasks: categorizing news as true or false, identifying its ideological stance, and determining its category. Our algorithm uses a multi-task learning model, incorporating contextual information to enhance detection performance. We evaluated and compared the effectiveness of our approach with existing methods by conducting experiments on real datasets. Our results show that incorporating contextual information is a superior strategy, outperforming the current best method by over 3% in terms of the F1 score.

Thermodynamic theory encounters an obstacle when applying it to complex systems that behave dynamically and have multiple stable states, due to the absence of a well-defined curvature effect. Our study reveals that when the thermodynamic formalism is applied correctly, using the natural Riemann metric, the thermodynamic parameters of these systems behave consistently. As a result, the hysteresis that these systems exhibit when their parameters change rapidly can be understood more clearly. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the rate at which the entropy of these systems changes over time is directly related to the negative curvature of their invariant sets.

We address the L1-PCA problem that suffers from curvature issues when using Nesterov's method. To bypass this limitation, we recast the problem into a two-block formulation with rotational invariance. We then develop a proposed algorithm that leverages this formulation and employs a combination of alternating updates with extrapolation. We prove that our method achieves a linear convergence rate and obtains an $\mathcal{O}(1/t)$ convergence rate for L1-PCA, outperforming the best available result for standard L1-PCA. When applied to a rotated and constrained version of the problem, known as the L1-kmeans problem, our method also exhibits strong performance. When comparing our method to the current state-of-the-art results for standard L1-PCA, we find that it converges at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/t^2)$ when the population variance is known and at a rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/t)$ when the population variance is unknown.

To validate the quality of annotated data, this study suggests using paraphrase tasks to compare similar data points. However, to ensure objectivity, the method used should be independent of the original annotation. For instance, using a human judge to compare annotated data, rather than relying on the original annotators. When multiple annotators contributed to the data, this method can also evaluate the inter-annotator consistency. To achieve this, our approach involves training a semantic labeling model on a large, lightly annotated dataset, and then applying the model to a smaller, more detailed annotation set, which is then compared pairwise by human judges. By doing so, we can validate the consistency of the annotations across different levels of detail, as well as the consistency between different annotators. Our experiments showed that the approach is effective in assessing the quality of annotations, particularly when compared to the traditional method of using gold standard comparisons.

A emerging challenge in cooperative navigation systems is how multiple agents can share knowledge to achieve efficient path planning, particularly when they have different speeds and mapping information. Existing solutions typically rely on agents contributing to a central, globally accurate map to guide their navigation. However, maintaining a centralized map can be impractical due to the need for frequent updates and synchronization among the agents. In contrast, our proposed HiTMap framework enables multiple mobile agents to effectively navigate independently, each with their own local map, by sharing proximal map fragments. We've developed a computational model and tested it simulated and real-world scenarios, demonstrating that our method efficiently manages navigation by prioritizing updates of locally relevant map information.

Our research found that, using atomic interferometry, a very weak local magnetic field could be detected with extremely high sensitivity. We demonstrated that the effect of a local magnetic field, as minimal as $10^{-17}$ tesla, can cause a noticeable shift in the frequency of atomic interference patterns. This achievement holds the record for the highest magnetic field detection limit in a laboratory setting. This sensitive detection capability allows for precise measurements of local magnetic fields near sensitive instruments, such as atomic clocks. We have also established that, under ideal conditions, the minimum detectable magnetic field is directly proportional to the square root of the atom number, a finding that we confirmed through experiments with various large ensembles of atoms.

We analyze a Bayesian nonparametric model for admixture decomposition, which utilizes Dirichlet processes to create a hierarchical structure for densities. Our investigation focuses on a specific model where the Dirichlet process prior on densities results in exchangeable admixture weights. We prove that when only relative order information about the components is known, the posterior distribution's support consists of scenarios where the admixture weights are not identifiable, and we show that conditioning on the absolute order of the components restores uniqueness of the admixture weights. Furthermore, our investigation reveals that this model can be viewed as a special case of a more general model with non-exchangeable admixture weights, which enables the recovery of a specific pattern of Dirichlet prior parameters that signals uniqueness of the admixture weights.

Dynasoor, a highly innovative, externally visible, and high-performance GPU memory allocator, has been developed to address the intricate memory management requirements of contemporary high-performance computing workloads featuring massive datasets. Unlike conventional, self-contained GPU memory allocators that utilize internal fragmentation to prevent memory leaks, Dynasoor externalizes memory management through a page-based approach, thereby significantly reducing memory waste and both system and application overhead. Benefiting from a sophisticated, multi-threaded, lock-free design, Dynasoor also exhibits exceptional performance, outstripping leading open-source GPU memory allocators by up to 3 times in various benchmark tests. Moreover, Dynasoor's streamlined memory management strategy enables it to handle large-scale applications with ease, successfully managing large memory allocations of up to 32 gigabytes in various benchmark scenarios.

Researchers analyzed the behavior of Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) states within the context of a one-dimensional chain, focusing on interactions and spin configuration caused by magnetic adatoms or dimers at the chain's edges. A generic model was developed to assess the spin-orbit coupling's impact on the chain's spectrum. By adjusting the inter-site coupling from strong to weak, scientists observed significant changes in the positions of YSR state peaks. When considering pairs of magnetic adatoms with antiferromagnetic coupling, not all YSR states disappeared as expected, and spin-orbit coupling caused some states to shift and others to merge. A comparison with previous studies revealed that the combination of free and coupled YSR states in chains with paired magnetic adatoms or dimers is not a singular phenomenon. It was also observed that the distribution of charge within paired magnetic adatoms or dimers can fluctuate with the spin configuration, potentially leading to magnetic configurations that could be realized through experimental means, such as microwave spectroscopy.

A transition from mini-Neptunes to Earth-like planets could be identified within a specific range of sizes (1.8 to 2.5 times the size of Earth) by examining how planets with Earth-sized interiors cross their host star's light. Among the thousands of super-Earths and sub-Saturn exoplanets discovered, few have been large enough to potentially harbor conditions suitable for life. Two exoplanets, Kepler-452b and K2-240b, stand out from the majority of small planets discovered by NASA's Kepler mission. To better understand these planets' characteristics and habits suitability, researchers studied and refined the details of Kepler-452b and K2-240b using various techniques, including analyzing light patterns created when these planets pass in front of their host stars. Although previous studies established Kepler-452b as a likely candidate for hosting life, our more precise measurements confirmed its size and shape, in addition to positioning it within its host star's temporary "doughnut" zone. Similarly, our analysis of K2-240b revealed its likely composition, shape, and position relative to its star's "doughnut" zone, which may support life on a partially liquid, Earth-sized core.

To analyze the atomic arrangement of dopants and vacancies in TiO2, we used classical empirical potentials via molecular dynamics simulations. Our study examined various scenarios: substitutional carbon and nitrogen in TiO2, interstitial carbon and nitrogen, and single and triple vacancies of oxygen. We found that interstitial dopants prefer the 4cp site near the Ti atom, while substitutional dopants prefer the 2cp site, which results in different electronic properties. Additionally, we found that interstitial vacancies tend to aggregate with each other and with interstitial dopants, and that experimental techniques such as NMR and XAS are more likely to detect these atoms rather than the substitutional ones.

An analysis at the LHC of top quark flavor changing neutral current decays via semi-elastic processes in top quark pair production is presented. This study considers various final state signatures involving one isolated lepton, missing energy, and additional jets. Utilizing 20fb−1 of proton-proton collision data collected by the CMS and ATLAS experiments, upper limits are set on rare decays of the top quark into neutral bosons or quarks. For a neutral scalar particle with a mass of 20 GeV, the upper limit on the branching ratio is found to be 1.5×10−4 in the CMS experiment and 2.5×10−4 in the ATLAS experiment, both based on 5σ statistical significance. Similar limits are derived for a neutral pseudoscalar particle and a Z boson, and the predicted rates for rare top quark decays in various new physics scenarios are discussed.

It has been proven that in triangle-free graphs, the desired color scheme uses no more than $\Delta+2$ colors, where $\Delta$ represents the highest degree of any vertex in the graph. A notable unsolved problem arises when considering triangles and asks it to determine the minimum number of colors needed for this distance representation, with no other restrictions imposed. Qubits based on harmonic oscillators can be used to measure masses with a precision potentially exceeding $10^{-20}$ times the mass unit. However, the reliability of this method is compromised when implementing it, as it introduces random measurement errors. Our study compares the robustness of this mass-measurement technique in both qubits and qutrits, subjecting it to various types of random measurement fluctuations that distort measurements. We found that qutrits can resist the degradation of precision more effectively, specifically under certain types of errors, but ultimately both qubits and qutrits will lose their precision at the same rate when the measurement errors become too unreliable. Nonetheless, qutrits demonstrate an advantage when the noise that causes the random fluctuations is confined to specific ranges, thereby offering an alternative for implementing mass-measurement precision that is similarly robust but based on three-level systems.

The polarization of positrons has significant implications for their utility in physics research, specifically in context of dedicated experiments that utilize positron beams. According to a finding presented in the paper, it is feasible to achieve polarization degrees greater than 30% among positrons, a threshold considered crucial for several experiments, by utilizing polarized electron beams with the correct characteristics. This goal can be achieved by employing radiation from recollisions that are optimized through a combination of appropriate photon energies and long wakefields. The study demonstrates that the polarization modulation that occurs in radiofrequency cavities can be a significant issue, but it may be mitigated by designing the electron beam in a particular way to minimize polarization modulation while maintaining suitable charge levels. The paper also highlights the potential for dedicated experiments that utilize positron polarization, in addition to highlighting the possibility of polarized positron production for dedicated experiments that utilize converted photons, such as the one being developed at Jefferson Lab.

We establish the existence of a finite group that exhibits polynomial diameter growth across its infinite conjugacy classes, has a non-trivial largest nilpotent subgroup, and does so in a relatively compact space, thus addressing several conjectures proposed by Breuillard and Duchesneau.

A novel, ultra-low-voltage temperature sensor has been created using a single CMOS transistor and a gate-only parasitic diode. This sensor operates at an extremely low power consumption of 7fJ/K^2 and provides a high degree of accuracy with a 1.4°C RMS temperature resolution and a -0.8°C bias point inaccuracy over a broad temperature range (from -20°C to 80°C). Its compact design consists of only two transistors and has a minimal area of 10x10µm, making it suitable for a wide range of Internet of Things (IoT) applications.

A topological groupoid extension can be viewed as a topological stacky extension, whose underlying abstract structure corresponds to extensions of topological groupoids that are equivariant with respect to mappings into a given topological stack. This observation leads to an equivalence between extensions of topological groupoids and extensions of functors, with the latter being defined as mappings of functors that are natural with respect to mappings of topological spaces. This understanding further implies that gerbes over topological stacks are equivalent to collections of extensions of topological groupoids along mappings of topological spaces.

A statistical analysis of 71 molecular cores was performed across two nearby, massive star-forming regions using high-density transformation modeling and spectral line data. Our findings show that core mass growth rates are directly correlated with the formation of massive stars: a significant majority (84%) of stars with $2.5 \leq \mathrm{M}_\mathrm{core}/\mathrm{M}_\sun \leq 10.0$ formed from cores with growth rates exceeding $10^{-7}\, \mathrm{M}_\sun \, \mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, whereas no such connection exists with the core's initial mass. Additionally, we observed a direct, nonlinear relationship between mass growth and luminosity, as well as an inverse, linear relationship with the core's free-fall collapse time. Notably, we discovered that turbulence plays a more substantial role in mass growth than temperature does. Our research suggests that massive star formation is unlikely within the observed set of molecular cores, with only one core exhibiting a mass growth rate high enough for this outcome (a probability of 0.03 or 3%).

To extend classical differentiation and integration to general zonal functions, we must first establish stronger differentiability properties and show that differentiating or integrating such functions results in zonal functions that maintain their positive definiteness. To accomplish this, we will utilize the theory of special Hermite polynomials and hypergeometric functions, enabling a deeper understanding of their connections to zonal functions. By applying these connections, we can demonstrate the desired differentiability and integrability properties and prove that the resulting zonal functions, when transformed through specific Dickson-Hermite transforms, yield explicitly defined classical operators that preserve positive definiteness.

The relationship between fluid flow and foam structure is influenced by the size and arrangement of bubbles, which affects the surface area of the foam's top layer. Researchers have begun analyzing these effects by creating mathematical models that account for varying levels of roughness, represented by a factor that compares the actual surface area to the ideal, perfectly smooth surface area. Studies have demonstrated that this roughness factor plays a critical role in determining the viscosity of liquid foams during flow. To further understand its significance, additional research is necessary, considering factors such as bubble size distribution and the forces driving their coalescence. Given the limited scope of existing research, extending it to include non-elasto-plastic behavior and more complex flow simulations is essential.

Deep ensemble methods, which involve creating multiple versions of a
convolutional neural network and combining their predictions, have been shown
to deliver superior performance in various image classification tasks. Our research
explores ways to enhance ensemble classifiers through a novel, two-component
approach, one part being a feature extraction module and the other a classifier
module. By applying our method to ResNet, we observed a notable improvement
in performance, with a significant reduction in the number of parameters required
for training. Our two-component framework may be applied to other ensemble
methods to enhance their performance.

We investigated the complex behavior of a thin liquid membrane within a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, characterized by the interplay of membrane tension, rotation rate, and perfusion flow rate. The stability of the membrane's various states was examined through numerical simulations, revealing non-linear relationships between the membrane's behavior and these parameters. The model demonstrated how increased membrane tension can influence the membrane's stability, as well as the rotation rate and flow rate, in different scenarios. The results also showed how the membrane can exhibit different stability characteristics in rotating frames of reference. The model's findings were validated through comparison with previously obtained analytical results and demonstrate the importance of considering membrane tension and rotation reference frames in understanding the behavior of membrane states.

Cyclopentadiene's CCH to CN abundance ratio shows a larger than expected 5.5 fold increase compared to benzene, whose CCH to CN abundance ratio is significantly lower at approximately 1.3. This distinction is particularly notable in the infrared spectra of its interstellar medium counterparts and may provide a notable signal that could aid in identifying cyclopentadiene within the Milky Way, though further verification is necessary. Based on current observations, it's clear that cyclopentadiene and benzene have different formation pathways, which is supported by the observed differences in their abundance ratios and can be attributed to the presence of oxygen in cyclopentadiene that inhibits its ring stability and leads it down a different chemical pathway.

To enhance the performance of neural machine translation, a novel look-ahead attention mechanism is proposed, which directs the attention towards the predicted next attention position instead of the actual output. This approach prevents the model from being distracted by less important parts of the sentence that may have high scores due to partial context. To obtain the predicted next attention position, a simple yet effective method is proposed, which utilizes the expected output based on the current context and the source sentence. This expected output is modeled as the mean of the future output, which can be either a fixed vector or a function of the source sentence. The proposed look-ahead attention mechanism is evaluated and shows significant improvements when combined with conventional attention mechanisms in the baseline models.

The rapid evolution of grid computing is being driven forward through the integration of foreign technologies. Despite its effectiveness, this approach has limitations when it comes to scalability. A proposed method aims to adapt a translational approach, typically employed in software development, to enhance grid computing. This method involves creating a bridge between the description of grid services and their programming language counterparts. A question arises as to whether this approach can facilitate seamless service integration as claimed. A grid-based service integration experiment was conducted to provide an empirical basis for evaluating this claim. The results showed that the method does indeed facilitate service integration but only to a certain extent. Furthermore, the findings revealed that the method may lead to unnecessary code translations, resulting in increased execution times. A possible improvement is also suggested, involving the use of a common intermediate language.

We developed a novel cosmological model based on an expanded F(R) gravity theory, describing the visitous nature of gravity. The model includes an additional parameter, allowing for a constant term that can affect the present universe's evolution, in a way that may resemble the effects seen in $Λ$CDM. By applying the model to a set of observational datasets, including supernova, cosmic microwave background, and matter power spectrum, we found that it fits the data remarkably well without requiring any adjustment to the parameters of existing fundamental theories. Specifically, with a visitous coefficient of 10^(8) kg^-1, this model successfully matches the observations of the current universe's expansion rate and structure density. Additionally, with no extra free parameters, it aligns with the findings from galaxy clustering and neutrinoless double beta decay. If confirmed, this visitous coefficient could lead to visitous effects on the neutrino mass, enabling the possibility of determining the universe's visitous nature through next-generation experiments like the one planned for the Karlsruhe Institute of Physics.

Re-examining the Bannhan-Cohen-Drell-Gershtein-McDonald (BCDGM) model's assumptions and dark matter formalism, we found that the typically constrained dark matter-nucleon scattering cross-section may be overly conservative when considering the $J/\psi \to \text{invisible}$ process. This process is dominated by the $J/\psi$ meson annihilating into a dark matter pair, which then escapes undetected. By re-calculating the form factors for this process, we found that it leads to cross-section upper limits being two orders of magnitude more lenient when utilizing the BCDGM method. Alternatively, utilizing a phenomenological approach based on QCD properties of the $J/\psi$ meson can lead to cross-section limits two orders of magnitude more stringent. This distinction highlights the significance of model dependence in dark matter constraints from $J/\psi$ data.

Multi-scale fractional spectral-sine transform (MFSSA) is a cutting-edge image decomposition technique that leverages a unique combination of discrete and continuous transform properties. This study conducts a thorough mathematical exploration of MFSSA, developing a framework that applies the method to various problems and contexts. Our results demonstrate that MFSSA can be formulated as a linear combination of discrete Fourier transforms (DFTs), allowing it to be efficiently computed using established algorithms. A key finding shows that MFSSA can be viewed as a form of DFT, specifically fractional-sine DFT. This discovery unlocks the possibility of employing MFSSA in a wide range of applications, including the analysis of complex data curves, such as temperature curves, and image processing, including remote sensing. Our research also delves into the computational aspects and presents a simplified implementation of the MFSSA algorithm. Ultimately, our work provides a robust foundation for further advancements and innovations in MFSSA research.

This research examines a random walk with independently identically distributed (i.i.d.) zero-mean increments, and it determines under what conditions the asymptotic behavior of the walk's tail relies on the second moment of its step sizes. When the walk's steps have a finite second moment, it is found that the tail of its distribution asymptotically behaves like a Gaussian, whereas if the moments above 2 are finite, its distribution's tail asymptotically resembles a stable law of the same index as the walk's steps. Additionally, if the walk's steps have moments greater than 1 but infinitely many, its tail asymptotically resembles a Fourier transform of a $\gamma$ function, where the shape of this function depends on the walk's parameters. It is worth noting that previous studies on this subject required the walk's steps to have a finite p-th moment for some p greater than 1. The current study also addresses the case where the walk's origins are included in the distribution being analyzed, and it compares the asymptotic behaviors of the tail distributions from both the excluded and included perspectives. The study further explores how the inclusion of the walk's origins affects its asymptotic behavior, and it discusses the conditions under which the two definitions of tail distribution asymptotics coincide. The research presented in this paper is an extension of the studies found in recent literature on the subject, and it is an improvement over the approaches used in those studies. The research is also an extension of the works found in recent literature

This research analyzed the optimization of a plasma source for a specific application, focusing on two types of magnetron sputtering discharge: unbalanced and balanced. Unbalanced discharge was studied using a single uncoiled coil, and optimized parameters included capacitively coupled power, asymmetry factor, and plasma coverage. A response surface methodology was employed to identify the critical factors influencing plasma distribution. On the other hand, balanced discharge utilized two coiled coils, with optimized parameters being capacitively coupled power, asymmetry factor, and plasma density. Both unbalanced and balanced discharges were experimentally verified using a dual-target setup.

We propose a novel W-shaped network, dividing the image into anaxial, erect, and abaxial parts, to significantly improve the accuracy of automatic nucleus detection. Unlike conventional methods that process images in a straightforward manner, our technique takes advantage of the nucleus's typically central location. By splitting the image, we enable our network to focus on distinct aspects and orientations, thereby increasing efficiency. In our experiment, we concentrate on detecting nuclei in cytological images. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our model delivers a 36.4% reduction in detection time while maintaining a 0.3% difference in recall rate.

Let's consider odd special orthogonal groups, specifically $SO(2n+1,\mathbb{R})$ and $SO(2n+1,\mathbb{C})$, as well as the symplectic group $Sp(2n+1,\mathbb{C})$. This research aims to explore the properties of local gamma factors for glacial representations and demonstrate that under specific conditions, the rank of twists for local gamma factors can be determined and may result in an equality of representations. Additionally, we reexamine previous works by Langlands, Jacquet, Conrey, Goldstein, and Farmer to gain a deeper understanding of the subject matter.

Deep Neural Networks have seen significant advancements in various tasks, yet their underlying mechanics remains poorly understood. To gain insights, we analyze the structure of trained CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks using Graph Convolutional Networks. Our method maps the learned features to graph convolution filters and evaluates their effect on input data. Our approach is versatile and applicable to any network architecture, allowing us to recover precise specifications for their component layers. Our results demonstrate that CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks indeed employ graph convolution operations, with patterns of convolution revealing their internal mechanisms and implicitly capturing spatial and hierarchical information in their features. To validate our approach, we utilize our analysis to design and train more efficient networks, and our code is publicly accessible for further customization.

In $2+1$ dimensions, rotating hairy black holes share the same structure as their four-dimensional counterparts. An in-depth entropy analysis across Chern-Simons gravity variants reveals that the entropy of these black holes closely matches that of the standard Chern-Simons theory, except for a minor correction term. This finding can be further generalized to include variants of Einstein gravity, and our calculations also cover solutions with a cosmological constant in the probe brane model. Notably, our results demonstrate that the entropy formula $\frac{A}{4}$ applies universally, thereby confirming previous conjectures based on numerical and analytic data. Our work expands upon a previous entropy investigation, providing derivations through the Hawking temperature relationship and confirming that the entropy of rotating hairy black holes remains consistent with the conjectured relationship proposed by M. J. J. V. de Queiroz, A. Y. Puertas, and R. O. Santos.

Ultrasound elastography is a method used to visually represent tissue stiffness distributions across cross-sectional images. Axial and lateral stiffness measurements have different accuracy levels due to ultrasound signal encoding limitations. Research indicates that axial measurements are more reliable and account for system variations, whereas the accuracy of lateral measurements lags behind. The primary objective of this research is to develop a new axial-lateral combined estimation approach, axial-first then lateral, utilizing acoustic radiation force elasticity imaging and motion estimation. The proposed method was tested on numerical phantom data and real-world data from breast and liver tissues. The results from both synthetic and actual tissue data demonstrate the effectiveness of the suggested method, with estimation errors for axial and lateral displacements at 0dB compression reducing to 12.6% and 26.7% respectively, in comparison to 15.9% and 30.4% for the conventional approach.

Traditional programming pseudocodes frequently omit essential checks, assuming input correctness based on their intended purpose, which is not a viable standard for modern software. In contrast, logical pseudocodes prioritize rigorous specifications that ensure both effectiveness and safety, utilizing a formal logic framework. In this research, we define a method to automatically convert functional specifications into ring-based logical pseudocodes, ensuring that ring operations are correctly mapped, and we demonstrate this approach by creating pseudocodes for several well-known cryptographic functions, including hash-based and public-key encryption methods.

We introduce a one-pass algorithm for creating a small, high-performance dataset, known as a coreset, that can be used to estimate the optimal solution to the $k$-means clustering problem. This coreset is specially designed to operate within a predefined metric space and can determine the optimal solution when it is given in its entirety. We prove that our algorithm generates an effective coreset for a wide variety of metric spaces, including Euclidean spaces of any dimension. Unlike previously established approaches, our algorithm only requires a single pass through the data and uses a constant amount of memory. We further demonstrate that the size of the coreset we create is directly proportional to the square root of the number of data points, log base the number of clusters, and the dimension of the Euclidean space. We also present experimental findings that confirm the practical efficacy of our coreset generation algorithm.

In large-scale grid worlds, an agent can divide the environment into distinct regions, assigning a single label to each one, which we call "superstates." By doing so, decision-making becomes more manageable, reducing the need for detailed knowledge of the environment. However, the effectiveness of this approach depends on how the agent partitions the world, and a poor division may lead to suboptimal outcomes. We've found that a randomized and adaptive method of assigning superstates, which is based on local observations and learns from experience, produces better results compared to static and random partitioning methods. This approach, which we've tested in simulation scenarios with multiple agents and obstacles, yields significant improvements in achieving goals in pursuit-evasion games, especially when the agent has limited knowledge of the environment's layout.

A theoretical framework that generates parton distribution functions (PDFs) for W and Z bosons has been developed and used to calculate universal corrections to their production in high-energy collisions. Studies have confirmed that the impact of these corrections is significant, potentially influencing measurements made by the LHC and future colliders. This research expands upon a previous finding by reconciling the PDF PDF4WDM and the MMHT2014 PDF set through the implementation of PDF reweighting, and it also explores the effects of varying the W and Z boson masses within their respective uncertainty ranges. Two major developments have been announced recently: the official integration of the PDF4WDM suite into the PDF reweighting tool, PDFreweight, and the release of new PDF sets that incorporate corrected W and Z boson PDFs, tailored for the use in Monte Carlo event generators via the PDF set interface, along with instructions for usage.

To evaluate the performance of learned dynamics models in multi-task reinforcement learning, our study evaluates several key aspects. Initially, we test a single dynamics model on multiple related tasks and find that it can successfully generalize, albeit with certain challenges, such as the risk of it being too confident in its predictions. Additionally, we discovered that using a dynamics model to guide policy optimization in multi-task domain does not yield the expected benefits and may even lead to performance deterioration. However, using multiple dynamics models, each trained on their respective individual data without shared parameters, can significantly enhance performance and, in some cases, result equivalent to jointly learning from data and rewards. Our findings are accompanied by empirical data, alongside several possible explanations for our observations. Our code has been made publicly accessible on GitHub at the following URL: https://github.com/ghy4y4/LDDMR.

We derive a formal system, akin to Peano Arithmetic, which we'll call PA+, and demonstrate that any non-trivial, formal system similar to PA+ cannot prove or disprove a specific, first-order logical statement regarding its own consistency. This shows that a heightened form of Godel's first incompleteness theorem is valid, where a heightened version of beta-formula F, which asserts the non-existence of a certain kind of proof within the system, is undecidable and cannot be established as true or false through the system itself.

This study expands Hadamard's three circles theorem to reflect its more comprehensive analog in real dimensions two, three, and four, as hypothesized by a higher order Riemann Hypothesis. To achieve this, new construction methods are introduced, involving a specific type of monogenic function based on orthogonal polynomials, and leveraging the Clark-Omortz rule. A connection is established between these constructions and the Cauchy-type operators in several complex variables.

Imaging the underlying structure of a population based on sparse, representative data points is a complex task. To efficiently navigate this challenge, we develop a method called regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN (RCW-GAN) to accurately generate posterior samples. This novel approach, inspired by the conditional Wasserstein distance, adds a regularized term to the standard WGAN objective function. The result is an interpretable model that captures the posterior distribution of data points, enabling the generation of posterior samples. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our RCW-GAN model by applying it to two complex tasks: recovering the distribution of natural images from uniform noise, and reconstructing the spatial distribution of tumors from limited MRI scans.

This research paper examines the concepts of invariance and robustness in linear fractional time-varying systems. The issue of invariance is addressed first, where we consider subspaces $M$ and define an error function $e(t,x(t),u(t))$ as the distance between a system state and the desired subspace. The paper then delves into finding conditions for subspaces $M$ and $\hat{M}$ to be invariant with respect to the system and its uncertainty, and includes robustness analysis via the use of a set of reachable states from those initial conditions considered safe. The problem of maintaining invariance is then formulated as ensuring that the error function remains non-negative, and this issue is approached using a Lyapunov function to guarantee that the error function's derivative is non-positive. The article also explores the application of this methodology to a mass-damper-system and highlights the time-varying nature's impact on invariance and robustness.

Twenty-one screen-like scattering sites from the direction of PSR B1133+16 have been observed twenty-seven times over nine years. We have identified twenty-one strong scintillation components that appear consistently across multiple observations. Although some components show variations in brightness and some others in position, most remain relatively stable. We have monitored the components' behavior for up to five years and have observed small changes in their distances from Earth. For one component, we have precise measurements of its distance changing by about 0.3 astronomical units over a period of seven years, a phenomenon that has never been observed before. Most components' velocities across the line of sight are very small, at approximately 0.0004 light-years per year. We have calculated the densities within the components' paths and found them to be similar, at approximately 10^1-10^2 particles per cubic light-year. We have also calculated the sizes of the components, which range from 0.000003 to 0.00007 parsecs in length and 0.000006 to 0.00014 parsecs in width. We have observed that the components do not occupy the same regions as some interstellar medium channels, which could imply that the scattering screens and the channels are distinct entities with different properties.

To effectively model speech signals that contain quasi-periodic components, a proposed convolutional neural network structure incorporates a cascaded design, separating the analysis and synthesis stages. Unlike standard convolutional networks that directly produce frequency bin outputs, this method uses a initial set of frequency bins as inputs to multiple analysis modules, which then input the results to synthesis modules to generate the final output spectrum. A proposed recursive sub-band division technique is used to enhance the analysis modules, allowing the network to accurately capture speech components across multiple frequencies. When applied to the task of speech enhancement, this cascaded network architecture achieves a 5.8 dB improvement in the signal-to-bias ratio (SBR) compared to a conventional convolutional neural network.

We introduce a topological Hochschild homology (THHH) construction for weak monoidal functors defined within the context of bicategorical topology. This extension allows us to incorporate the inherent symmetries of monoidal structures and, as a result, our THHH theory becomes capable of detecting aspects of bicategorical functors that are beyond the scope of traditional HH theories. By leveraging topological properties, our approach can also utilize fundamental properties of the functors in question, effectively yielding a theory that is both intrinsic and descriptive. The development of THHH is complemented by a thorough examination of its underlying properties and a notable corollary is derived, which can be viewed as a refined incarnation of Rognes' Shadows conjecture.

VGG-Sound Source is a comprehensive new dataset that encompasses a wide range of auditory source categories, a pioneering achievement in the field of sound classification. VGG-SS stands out from other existing datasets in its broad scope, consisting of 125 distinct auditory source classes, with over 12,000 high-quality 10-second recording examples for each class, carefully curated from open source platforms. To further enhance the utility of this dataset, we have developed a robust baseline model that can train on just 20% of the data and achieve impressive performance on the remaining 80%, with results that surpass those on current sound classification datasets, including VGG-Sound. VGG-SS is a versatile dataset that can be used to train and evaluate models in a wide range of real-world applications, including the classification of animal sounds, music genres, and industrial noises, among many others. To facilitate widespread adoption and future innovation, we are openly providing the dataset, as well as a pre-trained model, without any licensing fees or restrictions.

To tackle the challenge of representing high-dimensional node features in graph convolutional networks, we consider a hypersphere characterized by multiple dimensions and develop a new framework called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN). Our proposed method first applies a novel data augmentation technique to extend the realm of available data beyond its current dimensionality, allowing for the incorporation of more dimensional data without the need for feature normalization. Furthermore, we introduce a non-linear pooling module to aggregate neighbor representations and design an advanced graph convolutional layer to facilitate inter-domain information exchange. Through comprehensive experiments on 7 datasets with up to 26 dimensions in each node feature, our LGCN model consistently outperforms existing hyperbolic GCNs in terms of both accuracy and convergence speed, demonstrating the versatility and effectiveness of our approach.

This research paper examines the numerical solution to a nonlinear inverse problem for the 1D Euler-Poisson equation, where the implementation uses finite differences and relies on a stability estimate derived from a Carleman weight. Theoretical and computational results demonstrate the effectiveness of the Carleman-weight-based approach in overcoming ill-posed issues.

Complex systems in social contexts, which adhere to specific patterns of behavior, can be analyzed using the Tsallis distribution. Despite being an information-based entropy model, the Tsallis distribution's fundamentals remain rooted in thermodynamics. We reinterpret the Tsallis distribution's parameters from the perspective of Boltzmann's statistical mechanics, providing a clear pathway to their extraction directly from probability data. A straightforward statistical approach is also presented to calculate the Tsallis distribution's entropy, which is then applied to generate simulated data sets for verification.

The linearized gravity theory is analyzed under a general coordinate transformation, where the inclusion of a mass term in gravitational perturbations is allowed. Using a covariant Lagrangian approach, we employ a direct method to linearize general relativity and identify the degrees of freedom in the perturbed gravity regime. Through a consistent degree of freedom analysis, we determine the conditions under which the scalar degree of freedom is absent, and we find these conditions are equivalent to those derived using the direct method. However, we note that a mass term cannot be added to the Lagrangian if we start from a covariantly defined Fierz-Pauli action, as it would result in an inconsistent degree of freedom analysis. Conversely, if we commence with a massive gravity Lagrangian proposed by Damour, Dyda, and Scheel, then our consistent degree of freedom analysis reveals that the scalar degree of freedom remains present, despite being ghostly.

For classical and quantum systems, extending the concept of equilibrium states to include Hamiltonian dynamics has been well established. However, when considering quantum equilibrium states, there are actually four categories, each requiring a distinct definition. In this study, we analyze classical and quantum equilibrium states associated with specific quantum equilibrium states, referred to as the quantum Gibbs state. Our examination includes quadratic Hamiltonians, for which we determined the corresponding classical equilibrium states and observed that they represent averages of equilibrium states with respect to the system's energy spectrum. Additionally, we demonstrated that classical equilibrium states related to the quantum Gibbs state are insensitive to changes in temperature. Our research also involves developing a relevant quantum classical correspondence, thereby shedding light on the classical analogs that underlie equilibrium dynamics.

A common analogy for illustrating negative temperature involves a classical two-level system, where the energy levels can be thought of as being stacked in a vertical line, and the population is distributed between them. We can imagine trying to pour the population from the higher level to the lower one, defying the usual behavior associated with it, where the population naturally flows from a higher energy level to a lower one. We can consider this two-level system as a model for two energy levels within which particles can transfer between, and by examining it through the lens of quantum mechanics, we can see that it's feasible for two energy levels to have negative temperature in relation to each other. In our discussion, we'll focus on a specific scenario involving two quantum-mechanically coupled, classical two-level systems, and show that even when the individual components have positive temperatures, it's possible to achieve a situation where the two energy levels have negative temperatures in relation to each other, and we can visualize this using the two-level system analogy mentioned above.

A minimal dark sector model is developed using a dark parity symmetric framework that incorporates a dark parity symmetric version of the type-II seesaw mechanism. This model allows a minimal extension of the standard model, incorporating a real scalar dark sector that interacts via a Yukawa-driven splitting of masses. As a result, dark parity symmetry is maintained, and the stability of the vacuum is ensured. Furthermore, this minimal extension enables consistent dark parity symmetry and dark sector interactions that may be tested through future particle physics experiments. This work also explores two scenarios for the dark sector: one in which its particles remain elusive, and another in which it interacts strongly, and it identifies potential signatures for both cases within the parameter space that could be explored through experiments at the next generation of colliders, such as the Future Circular Collider.

To understand the behavior of transition metal oxides, it's crucial to assess spin-orbit coupling, which can result from both local electronic interactions and the specific crystalline structure. By utilizing a combination of cluster expansions and Monte Carlo simulations, researchers have analyzed spin-orbit coupling in simple two-dimensional lattices made of $d^2$ or $d^4$ electrons. The effective spin-orbit coupling strength was found to vary significantly, depending on the distance from a critical point that separates two phases with distinct crystal field patterns. The study also reveals that local exactness, along with the properties of magnetic moments and crystal fields, can serve as reliable order parameters for assessing the approach to these phase boundaries. The rigorous analysis allows for comparing results from different methods and theoretical predictions with experimental findings in materials like cuprates and iridates.

We define a new relative $I$-function for toric complete intersections with smooth divisors, demonstrating how a previous relative $I$-function formulation can be reinterpreted as an extension of sorts. Furthermore, we establish a fundamental relationship between these relative $I$-functions, facilitated through a toric complete intersection-specific version of an extended Kontsevich-Zagier formula. This connection enables us to computationally determine the coefficients of our new relative $I$-functions using toric methods, and we find that these coefficients correlate with Calabi-Yau threefolds' BPS invariants. By examining our relative $I$-functions through the lens of expansion properties, we derive formulas that directly link the invariants of Calabi-Yau threefolds to specific configurations of hyperplane classes within polytopes, and we demonstrate that these formulas collectively comprise a higher-dimensional Dolgachev's conjectural structure, with specific cases yielding the Genus Formula for curves and the Complete Intersection Formula for Calabi-Yau threefolds.

To advance medical imaging analysis, we believe that incorporating structured semantic manipulation into generative models is a promising approach. Our research builds on this concept by developing a medical image generation method that allows us to modify specific organs within an image. To achieve this, we created a custom conditional generative adversarial network (CAGAN) with a novel design that separates the coded representation into distinct, manipulable streams. By fine-tuning these separate codes, we can generate new images featuring altered organs. Our model's performance is demonstrated through a realistic and controllable generation of abdominal organs from MRI scans. The innovative design of our network was validated through comparative experiments, and we found that it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of FID score. Our code was developed using Python 3.7, PyTorch 1.7, and is publicly available on GitHub.

A new software program called ViDaExpert has been created to facilitate the
analysis of multidimensional data. This user-friendly tool allows users to easily
visualize and manipulate their data, making it simple to identify patterns and
outliers within their dataset. ViDaExpert supports a variety of file types and
can perform calculations, sort and filter data, and provide graphical representations
to aid in understanding the data. The program also supports decision tree-based
models and can handle missing data values. Developed using Java, ViDaExpert is a
free, open-source application that can be run on any platform supported by
Java. The authors of ViDaExpert invite users to contribute to its development and
suggest trying the program to explore its features and benefits.
